description: Stage directions were not included in brackets and were typeset in the printed text, appearing either before or within dialogue. When placed after dialogue, they were flush right on the same line if space allowed, otherwise moved to the next line. If spanning two lines, they were indented as hanging paragraphs with varying indentation amounts. In the etext version, all stage directions not located before or within dialogue are moved to the next line, indented the same amount as hanging paragraphs, and formatted consistently. These directions were never enclosed in brackets and followed specific layout rules to maintain clarity and readability in both printed and digital versions.

The Dean is surprised by a mention in *The Times* of seven wealthy people, including three brewers, each donating a thousand pounds to restore the Minster Spire, which he claims is only slightly out of repair and thus does not warrant such a large contribution. He believes the relief will be felt only tomorrow and considers the involvement of the brewers unjustified. The Dean had only fifty pounds for sporting purposes and instructed Blore to back Dandy Dick on behalf of the Restoration Fund, though Blore denies doing so, claiming it was done for the Dean’s sake. The Dean will be celebrated in sporting papers for backing Dandy Dick and is anxious to receive today’s *Times*. Georgiana offers to lend him a thousand pounds on condition he admits there is no harm in being mocked as a "sporting dean." The Dean owes the Restoration Fund money and has bills to settle, though he includes himself among estimable worthy men who do not possess a thousand pounds.

The speaker, a promising youth at college, reflects on a past incident where he obtained poison a month ago to kill a black retriever that fell from a hill, realizing now that the poison is in his pantry and could not have been used for cooking. He plans to carry out the act and steals out unseen by the Dean. Sir Tristram and Hatcham enter by the window carrying the Dean, who appears to have survived a prolonged struggle and describes feeling torn to fragments, likening his life to bills and spires in Oxford. The Dean recognizes Georgiana as his sister and asks where the drugs are. Tris waves her handkerchief, urges the group to proceed, and reminds them to mind the gate-post. Sheba and Salome appear outside the window, and SHEBA instructs that entry can be made via the window using a hairpin. The speaker later embraces the Dean, asks him to confess, and declares that true English sport has noble value.

The scene takes place in a domestic setting at Durnstone, where SHEBA, SALOME, TARVER, and DARBEY discuss preparations for a dinner. TARVER expresses depression over dressing like Charles the First, which SALOME praises, calling him Charles the First. DARBEY humorously refers to TARVER as a martyr to his liver, suggesting Charles the Martyr as a theme. SHEBA and SALOME express excitement about appearing magnificent. The men and women speak in undertones, indicating a private, humorous atmosphere. The Dean is present in the library and later leaves, expressing remissness. TARVER and DARBEY shake hands, with TARVER calling the evening fascinating and DARBEY calling it charming. DARBEY proposes meeting on Monday, but the Dean refuses, offering any time. The group later leaves, with SALOME and SHEBA dancing around the Dean. GEORGIANA enters, accusing TARVER of encouraging the girls, and Sir Tristram arrives, flattered by a kiss from Darbey.

The Dean, at the Deanery of St. Marvells, is concerned about a chill affecting the stable horse and decides to administer a Bolus as a humane precaution, relying on Blore for medical supplies. He recalls reading "The Horse and its Ailments" by John Cox, which he used to treat his old mare, and recognizes the book's remedy for chills. The Dean has not approached a horse medically in seven and twenty years and fears the Bolus may give competitors an unfair advantage, which he does not desire. He offers rest and forgetfulness at the Deanery, which includes household duties and a stable with a thirteen-year-old pony. Georgiana enters agitated, carrying an umbrella and candle, claiming she is overtrained and must satisfy herself, while Sir Tristram enters with an opened letter, announcing the bolus analysis has arrived. The Dean is indifferent to Georgiana’s confrontational behavior, claiming she enabled innocent babies to discharge an account for the first time. The Dean fears a chill from the rain and worries the stable is cramped if the animal becomes restive.

SHEBA and SALOME express frustration, with SHEBA wishing to borrow a brother and hating Nugent Darbey, wishing him to grow bald early, while SALOME mocks Gerald Tarver’s nose and wishes it deepens to frighten cows. DARBEY and TARVER enter dressed as Cavaliers, apologizing to Miss Jedd. Noah claims he is the only one who can withdraw charges and accuses the unknown person of alienating his wife’s affections, planning to drive them to Durnstone with evidence. Georgiana refuses to marry Sir Tristram, stating love is founded on mutual esteem, and claims he reared her when he touched her hand, as he did not place her brother’s head in a nose-bag; Sir Tristram denies wrongdoing, calling the actions common courtesies of everyday life. The Dean identifies Sir Tristram as the unknown person from the previous night, withdrawing any charge and attributing him innocent intentions. In the text, several commas are changed to semicolons on specific pages, and an apostrophe is omitted in the play text.

Aunt Tidman is described as a sad, broken, weary, and wave-tossed person, having suffered retribution from ill luck that devastated her horses, stock, and possessions, leading to their sale at auction. The Dean warned Sheba and Salome that they would find her in this state and that their task would be to win back a flickering smile from her wan features. Sheba and Salome, who are referred to as weary fragments, believe they owe forty pounds to Aunt Tidman, unknown to Pa, and express concern about money, with Sheba asking Georgiana if she knows something about the Races. Sheba claims Aunt Tidman does not flicker a smile at her, and Salome says she wouldn’t be in her shoes for anything. Georgiana confirms Aunt Tidman has had many troubles, and Sir Tristram notes another charge involving Georgiana’s stock. Noah suggests breaking the news of the speaker’s death to the girls during the evening, concluding it is an ordinary case of suicide.

Major Tarver is in a state of depression after forgetting his music and feeling he has incurred Miss Jedd's displeasure, leading to his failure to gain access to the race-course. He expresses love for Salome, which he claims has lasted eight weeks, and blames India for his emotional state. Darby, who takes responsibility for the Fancy Ball arrangements, plays the violin with Sheba accompanying him, while Salome sits beside Tarver. Tarver initially claims to have begun playing "Come into the garden, Maud" but discovers his music roll is empty. Darby describes Tarver’s love as second only to his own, particularly in how he looked at Sheba. Salome regrets her past remarks and insists on forgiving Tarver, though Tarver refuses to forgive her. Darby is seen enjoying life with Tarver, and Georgianas describes the evening as a pure, simple English Evening at Home. Tarver’s condition is critical, and he sinks onto the settee in despair. A boy is mentioned whose address is noted on an admission card, and Darby promises to wait for his mother’s explanation.

The dress bill for a flower girl totals forty pounds nineteen, comprising ten guineas for the skirt and bodice, five guineas for trimmings, and two guineas for extras. Sheba claims this amount is less than Salome’s and expresses regret over their lack of charity, while Salome states Papa has not paid the bill and is pressed for money. Sheba suggests getting Papa in a good humor and asking for money, noting he knows they haven’t been charitable. The Dean re-enters with a bundle of papers and repeatedly says "Bills!" as he examines them, stating he is "stumped-out of coin" and "run low." He is in handcuffs when Noah brings him out of a cell, and the Dean, though anxious, offers to be dealt with as desired. Salome and Sheba force the Dean into a chair, with Salome sitting on his legs and Sheba on the table, to present their father’s return. The Dean calls Sheba "Papsey" and instructs her to watch his carving at dinner.

Sheba and Salome, two young ladies, break a financial reserve by babbled for money at the Dean’s request, leading to his satisfaction and a discussion about their summer dress expenses. The Dean expresses love and solicitude for them but admits he has no spare cash, declaring they must retrench and rejoice if donors come. Salome and Sheba express fear and regret over the high cost of the fancy dresses, with Salome repenting upon seeing the account. Sheba believes Mr. Darbey is a small officer, accusing Salome of disrespect, while the Dean claims they have a distaste for Darbey. Darbey differs with the Dean and was about to make a witty remark before being interrupted. The Dean claims a remedy contains strychnine, sixteen grains, which horrifies the girls. After a scolding, Blore enters with letters and suggests hanging the scolding on the hatstand. Sheba says she will repent to-morrow, while Salome repents now. The Dean mentions the St. Marvell’s Spring Meeting, to be held the next day.

Georgiana, refusing to be called a lady, insists on helping clear the stables at the burning Old Swan Inn after Blore announces the fire and the gate-bell rings violently. The Dean stops her, reminding her of her status, but she persists. A conflagration is seen in the sky, and the characters react with alarm. Later, Georgiana points to the window, noting movement in the garden, not near the stables, and Sir Tristram confirms people are approaching the house. The Dean, concerned by a dreadful wave, hears footsteps in the garden and sees only the old spire against the threatening sky. He reproaches Georgiana, learns the horse is in the stables, and later goes into the garden to reflect. The fire is extinguished. The Dean is sure Mardon will lend him Sir Tristram’s coat and cap, which completely envelop and almost conceal him. Georgiana comments on Sheba’s stable companion, suggesting it could give her a stone and get its nose in front, a remark the Dean objects to as inappropriate.

Major Tarver, a middle-aged, tall, angular officer with a thin face, yellow complexion, and red eyes, is quartered at Mr. F. Kerr and has ridden from Durnstone to visit the Dean. Mr. Darby, a boy from Durnstone with a pompous and patronizing manner, accompanies him. Both are dressed in regimentals and enter the Dean’s home unannounced, appearing weak. The Dean, initially distracted, invites them to share a dinner of leg of mutton (hot) and custards (cold) at six o'clock on Tuesday night. Salome and Sheba, the Dean’s daughters, express anxiety and reproach him for his absence, while Sheba claims he has stooped to deception. Major Tarver, after a fit of illness, sings a line from a song and later claims indigestion. Dr. Middleton diagnoses him with a condition requiring a proposal to a lady or a seaside retreat. Georgiana notes Tarver’s lack of speech, suggesting liver issues, and Salome jokes that Gerald Tarver has no liver. Tarver later gasps upon seeing Salome, and the Dean recognizes his voice.

In St. Marvells, Noah, the head of the police station, is in charge of a case involving the disappearance of Dr. Jedd, the Dean of St. Marvells, who vanished after being last seen the previous night. Mrs. Tidman, introduced as Sir Tristram’s sister and Dr. Jedd’s sister, expresses fear at the police station and concern over her brother’s disappearance. Noah claims he took Dr. Jedd and accuses him of corrupting his profligate wife’s affections, though the Dean is later seen entering with Salome and other horses, and he hands Salome a copy of The Times showing he donated £1,000 to the Restoration Fund for Minister Spire. Sir Tristram disputes Noah’s account and insists on an official description of the Dean, which differs from Georgiana’s detailed one. Military personnel are stationed at Durnstone to prevent further unrest. The case is considered significant, possibly leading to newspaper coverage, though Hannah claims to know something about the arrest, while Blore denies any involvement, offering only a hypothetical suggestion to encourage hope.

Papa, described as a portly man of about fifty with a dignified demeanor, suave voice, persuasive manner, and noble brow surmounted by silver-gray hair, leaves the house at half-past nine with Blore, after which the house is quiet. He has been out all night, a fact that shocks Darby and Salome, who call it terrible and suggest not condemning him without hearing him out. Major Tarver, who had conceived the idea of distributing cast-off costumes in the middle of the night, arrives with plans to make final arrangements after parade, seeking to meet the Dean and buy gay songs. Tarver expresses excitement and relief at being accepted, though he suffers from alternating fits of despondency and acknowledges his liver is injurious. Salome fears Papa will hear them on the gravel path, and Tarver requests water with the least suggestion of cayenne pepper. The Army is described as not a bad sort and has trained nurses who, if sent with a perambulator, would fetch Tarver at half-past eight. Darby, on behalf of the Army, thanks Sheba, who believes he has a grand future.

Sheba, Salome, and Georgiana are friends who gather at the Deanery for dinners, where Sheba plays the piano and Georgiana pours tea. They describe a dinner as frightfully jolly, though the mutton was overdone and the custards were the cook’s first attempt. The dinner revealed the chimney needed sweeping. Georgiana notes it is a relief to shake off the gentlemen, though Salome and Sheba disagree. Sir Tristram Mardon is the Dean’s friend and Mrs. Tidman’s brother; the Dean recalls Mardon as rough and was once violently hit by Sir Tristram as a boy. At the Durnstone Athenaeum, two motherless girls were subjected to shock upon arriving, finding a notice on the front door reading: "Ball knocked on the head—Vivat Regina." Officers and gentlemen are blamed for responding to the call of duty, with Salome stating gentlemen inflicting agony on girls by being jeered at. The Dean appeals to Mardon, but Sir Tristram and Georgiana mock him, with Georgiana saying she will only consider him after two pails of water are thrown over him.

Salome and Sheba are two girls living under the care of a strict Dean, who accuses them of moral decay after they reveal winning fifty pounds at the races. The Dean refuses to accept their payment, insists they cannot cover the bill, and declares confidence between them is gone, withholding the reason for his absence. They consider how to help their poor, financially strained Papa, suggesting they play the piano when he is at work or steal out of the house with Major Tarver or Mr. Darbey—actions they believe would cause those men to die for them. Salome and Sheba whisper of an opportunity to ask Papa for money, both exclaiming "Poor dear Papa!" They reflect that if they had known their Aunt longer, they might have confided in her, but Sheba thinks it is poor to spoil her. The Dean believes abused institutions have redeeming traits but cannot reasonably ask the girls to organize a bazaar or concert. Georgiana, a visitor, touches the girls with her cane and asks them to kiss her. On page 97, the second "No" in "No, Aunt, No!" is changed to lowercase.

Georgiana Tidman, the Dean’s widowed sister, arrives at the estate after reconciling with him, bringing a mix of joy and tension. Described as jovial and noisy, she wears a billy cock hat and coaching coat, greeting the Dean as "Gus, my boy." She is welcomed as a second mother to the daughters, Salome and Sheba, though Sheba expresses reluctance. The Dean is disturbed by her arrival on the eve of the races at St. Marvells. Sir Tristram Mardon, a jovial sporting gentleman from Oxford, greets the Dean as "Jedd" and recalls their past friendship, noting he and Georgiana were students together. He insists on racing with his horse Dandy Dick, ridden by Tom Gallawood, and claims Bonny Betsy, a bay mare, cannot handle steep hills with a boy, though George Tidd—identified as Georgiana—had confidence in her strength. Blore is reprimanded for giving a mixture to Dandy instead of the Dean, and is ordered to remain in service as a sober, silent man. The Dean plans to drive to Durnstone to bring Georgiana over, while the daughters are surprised and uneasy about her presence.

Noah Topping, a dense, red-haired countryman dressed as a rural police constable, is a central figure in a play inspired by a real constable from a Brighton village. He is married to Hannah, who claims they have six years and ten months of marital duty, and asserts that all residents—including the Dean, the Durnstone Superintendent John Ruggles, and the Inspectors—belong to the "chapel folk." Noah plans to use the horse Old Nick to drive the Dean to Durnstone, claiming he can reach the hill’s edge in half the time. He forces Hannah to open the oven to release cooking smells into the stable, which she resists. The Dean, initially dismissive, later confesses that his only hope of avoiding a national calamity is to keep Hannah and the Superintendent in secret. Mr. Pinero developed the play’s central plot—a dean who becomes undignified after an indiscreet act—after being convinced by his dissatisfaction with his work and a suggestion from a rural constable. Mr. Clayton visited Brighton to hear Pinero read the play’s acts and returned with sketches, enabling the play’s rapid completion. The character of Noah Topping was directly inspired by the rural constable.

George Tidd is a person known for setting things square in a palace or puddle, with racing colors of crimson and black diamonds. Georgiana identifies as George Tidd and claims people at Newmarket will tell all about her, producing a crimson and black pocket-handkerchief. She instructs Blore to pack a hamper with cold chicken, French rolls, and two bottles of Heidsieck, labeling it 'George Tidd' and sending it to the Hill. The genial constable was bound to watch the races at the edge of the hill, up Pear Tree Lane. Georgiana discovers a plan by another woman and goes to the hill, where she finds hundreds of old friends, including welshers, pick-pockets, and card-sharpers, all part of the lowest racecourse cads. She feels at home among them, as comfortable as a duchess in a drawing room. Georgiana announces a relative has been caught for a three-card trick and invites people to rescue him at the brow of the hill, offering a pound each, possibly with six months added. The Dean, who initially opposes sport, acknowledges the races as a mental distraction and agrees to overlook Georgiana’s actions, though he vows never to allow such incidents again.

The DOOR, CELL DOOR, and GATE are central to several interactions. GEORGIANA opens the main DOOR to enter a police-station setting, where she and SIR TRISTRAM are admitted by HANNAH. A violent GATE BELL rings, prompting concern from SHEBA and SALOME, who fear it will wake PAPA. The CELL DOOR is used when the DEAN disappears through it after being confronted by NOAH, who locks it behind him. HANNAH unlocks the main DOOR multiple times, admitting GEORGIANA and SIR TRISTRAM, and later uses a large key to open the CELL DOOR to allow the DEAN entry. HANNAH, referred to as MRS. TOPPING, is central to domestic and procedural dynamics, expressing sorrow over the DEAN’s behavior and asserting that NOAH cannot put the horse to under ten minutes. NOAH, the constable, accuses the DEAN of embezzling a meal prepared by HANNAH and alienating his wife, Annah, and insists on taking further action at Durnstone. The GATE BELL, the DOOR, and the CELL DOOR serve as key points of tension and transition in the narrative.

A man is found trespassing in the Deanery Stables with intent to commit a crime, refusing to give his name or account; he opens the medicine chest, pours drops from bottles into a basin, counts three to six, and takes another bottle. Blore enters stealthily, whispers he has taken strychnine, empties a small paper packet into the basin, stirs it with a rolling-pin, and claims to have cooked Dandy Dick, expressing fear and guilt. When the Dean returns, he orders Blore to remove the substances and not be seen again that night. Blore defends the substance as merely an "orse," claims it was taken by the horse, and promises to retire from the Turf after tomorrow to reclaim it. The Dean recoils, takes the tray from Blore, and places it on the table, thanking him. Sir Tristram denounces the Dean as one of the most atrocious conspirators in the history of the Turf, citing his ownership of half of Dandy Dick.

Lewis Isaacs is a costumier to the Queen based at Bow Street, known for creating a gown from the period of the French Revolution in 1798, costing fifteen guineas for the gown and seven guineas for trimmings. The Dean is a debtor to Isaacs, with a total debt of forty pounds and nineteen shillings, which he claims reflects "imps of deceit" and links to a fancy masked ball at Durnstone. Aunt Georgiana married a man known as the Gentleman Jockey, who bred horses for racing and died ten years ago, leaving her a widow; she claimed he could be dislocated if he vexed her. She refused to allow betting on the horse Dandy Dick but agreed to let Sheba and Salome bet by placing petticoats on him, which frightened them. Sheba and Salome each wanted to win fifty pounds, with Sheba requesting forty pounds and nineteen shillings. The Dean, upon finding a document stating his debt, accuses the daughters of deceit and questions which was a person during the French Revolution, with Sheba pointing to Salome and the Dean claiming Salome was a flower-girl. The Dean later discovers bank-notes on his dressing-table totaling fifty pounds, which he intended to send to the bank.

The scene takes place in a country police station, specifically a Quain old room, which is partly furnished as a kitchen and partly as a police station. The room has plaster walls, oaken beams, and a gothic mullioned window. A massive door with a sliding wicket and iron grating opens to a prisoner's cell. Hannah, a young woman in a print gown, is cooking and singing gayly, calling out to Noah in another room. She asks if Noah will have dinner before driving the prisoner to Durnstone, to which he agrees. Noah is in a good temper over something and notes public characters are liable to irritation. The Dean invites Hannah and her husband to dine, offering a hot meal with ale; Noah criticizes Hannah for not thanking him, while she expresses gratitude by kissing his hands. HATCHAM arrives with a basin and bolus, claiming the villain who set fire to the 'Swan' administered a dose to the horse and has taken the constable to the lock-up, having knocked his collar. BLORE is in agony, stating they have taken the Dean.

Dandy, a horse, is central to the narrative, described as proud and distressed upon discovering it lacks a tail, a loss that causes emotional bereavement. Hatcham, a groom, expresses concern about Dandy, noting he has one mortal fear regarding the horse and suggests keeping the stable dark to prevent it from noticing the missing tail. Georgiana, who loves and clings to Dandy’s tail, believes it is an invalid part and sees the horse as a living example to a Dean. The horse survived a fire at the Swan, possibly incited by humans, and was harmed by cold water thrown upon it. Dandy won a handicap race in a common canter, with all others absent, and is now safe and sound. Georgiana fears thunder, which she associates with a dream in which Dandy sold himself to a circus and hooted after losing his tail, calling it an omen. Sir Tristram, who calls Dandy “Dandy Dick,” suggests swapping halves of the horse, but Georgiana refuses, saying she is a tender-hearted woman who loves the horse’s invalidity. The Dean, who is Georgiana’s brother, confirms the win and notes five hundred pounds will go to the Spire. A heavy roll of thunder is heard, and the Dean stirs pudding with a rolling-pin.

Dandy Dick is a horse owned half by Sir Tristram and half by Georgiana, who claims she does not own a whole horse but insists half is better than no bread; she secured her share through John Fielder, who sold it to Sir Tristram after she promised Augustin she would not own any four-legged animals. The Dean, a former race enthusiast, is tempted by a fifty-pound bet on Dandy Dick, an old horse with mahogany-like odds of ten to one, and places the bet with Blore, who later expresses surprise at the Dean’s passion and warns of a damaged professional relationship. Georgiana urges the Dean to raise fifty pounds, and both she and Sir Tristram are partners in managing Dandy Dick, with Sir Tristram taking him out of the Swan and Georgiana leading him into the Deanery. The play *Dandy Dick*, written by Arthur W. Pinero, is set at the Deanery of St. Marvells and performed 171 times before being transferred to Toole’s Theatre; it is considered the swan-song of the old Court Theatre and the partnership of John Clayton and Arthur Cecil. The play premiered at the Royal Court Theatre on January 27, 1887, and achieved success in Australia, limited success in America, and is noted for its comedic performance.

The Dean, played by Mr. G. W. Anson, is a central figure at St. Marvells, where he lives in a serene Deanery with a morning-room and garden. He is not a card player and is visited by Sir Tristram, who offers to teach him. The prisoner, taken in last night by Noah, is lodged in the "strong-box" cell, a space Hannah refers to as the cell itself. Blore, a visitor, claims the prisoner was brought to the stables and is now on premises, but Hannah denies seeing him and says Noah brought him home without her involvement. Blore expresses concern over the prisoner’s routine, including his shaving water and gaiters, and claims he has called on Hannah to respect him. Hannah refuses a kiss from Blore, recalling no social barriers when she was Miss Hevans. She is saddened by the Dean’s misfortune, which she learns Blore does not know of, and claims only she, her whistle, and Nick the fire-brigade horse know of it. The girls SALOME and SHEBA express anxiety about their "poor Papa" and how they were "led into it," with SHEBA saying it's a "scrape." The Dean is later seen leaving, and a character leaves him with a wish for calm and good luck, referencing Edward Blore’s "hide is shattered."

Georgiana and Gus are central figures in a world of races, deception, and familial bonds. Georgiana decides to clap Dandy Dick, a horse described as a moral certainty with a unique weight and tail, claiming no other horse matches him, and instructs Gus to keep this secret from the Canons and Archdeacons, warning they would shorten the price if they found out. She offers to make things right with Augustin (a name used for Gus by the Dean) and promises to lunch with the Canons and Bishop. Dandy Dick runs for the Durnstone Handicap and is described as fit as a fiddle, shining like a mirror. Georgiana has run many races with Gus, though they have never competed together, and both remain resilient despite being punished and pulled. Gus competes neck-and-neck with the Bishop and provides Georgiana with a dry stable and clean litter, keeping her out of the Shrewsbury and Talbot race. Georgiana distrusts Gus’s ability to handle a flying dogcart and expresses disbelief at his weight gain, calling him "my boy." She also notes that when Gus rides Deception, the horse takes the bit between its teeth and refuses to be stopped, with the Dean being the hardest rider. The spire is at risk of crumbling unless restoration begins, and Georgiana suggests a match between the Dean and the spire to settle bills.

Hannah Evans, wife of the erring constable, interacts with the Dean at the wicket, where he appears and disappears, and she identifies herself as Annah Topping, Knee Evans. She cries out upon seeing him, calling him her "old master," but he reveals he is the victim of a misfortune and has placed himself in an equivocal position. The Dean possesses the key to his handcuffs and the woman's whistle. He wishes to attest that the erring constable is the husband of a wife deserving respect and admiration, and gives Georgetana specific instructions: light the fire, prepare a warm bath and change of linen, and withhold judgment. Noah appears, questions the Dean about kindnesses from his wife, and learns of Hannah’s encounter with a gentleman through the wicket, whom she describes as speaking properly to a lady. Noah acknowledges the situation with irony, noting he has been given many new friends since moving to St. Marvells. The Dean recognizes Hannah as a former excellent cook and apologizes for her husband’s ignorance. Sir Tristram asks if the Dean has the key of his handcuffs, which he confirms he does.
